questions.question: What is autoboxing and unboxing in Java?
questions.title: Autoboxing and Unboxing in Java
questions.direct_answer: **Autoboxing** is the automatic conversion Java does when you assign a primitive (`int`, `double`, etc.) to its wrapper class (`Integer`, `Double`, etc.) — you write `Integer x = 5` and Java silently calls `Integer.valueOf(5)`. **Unboxing** is the reverse — when you use a wrapper object where a primitive is expected, Java calls `.intValue()` automatically.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand what autoboxing/unboxing actually is under the hood — compiler-generated calls to valueOf() and intValue() — and where it creates silent overhead.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking autoboxing is free. Every box creates a new object on the heap (except for the Integer cache -128 to 127). In tight loops this adds up.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that autoboxing can throw a NullPointerException during unboxing — if an Integer variable is null and Java tries to unbox it to int, it crashes. This is a subtle and common real-world bug.

sections.title: What the Compiler Quietly Does Every Time You Mix int and Integer
sections.content:
**Autoboxing** is Java automatically converting a primitive like `int` into its wrapper `Integer`, and **unboxing** is the reverse — turning an `Integer` back into an `int`.

Why does Java even need this? Because it has two parallel worlds. Primitives (`int`, `double`, `boolean`) are raw values that live on the stack and are fast. Wrappers (`Integer`, `Double`, `Boolean`) are real objects on the heap. The catch: **collections only hold objects**. You cannot write `ArrayList<int>` — generics need a class — so you write `ArrayList<Integer>`. Autoboxing exists so you can still drop a plain `42` into that list without manually wrapping it.

How does it work? The compiler does the conversion for you. When you write `Integer x = 5`, it silently rewrites it to `Integer x = Integer.valueOf(5)`. When you write `int y = x`, it rewrites it to `int y = x.intValue()`. You never see these calls, but they sit there in the bytecode.

One nuance worth knowing early: `valueOf()` keeps a small cache of `Integer` objects for the range `-128` to `127`, so two boxed values in that range can share one object — which is why `==` sometimes appears to work for small numbers and quietly fails for large ones.

And the gotcha that bites everyone: unboxing a `null` `Integer` throws a `NullPointerException`. A line like `int y = someInteger` becomes `someInteger.intValue()`, and calling a method on `null` crashes — even though the line looks like a harmless assignment.

sections.title: Autoboxing and Unboxing — What the Compiler Does
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart LR P["int 5
primitive on stack"] -->|"autoboxing
Integer.valueOf(5)"| W["Integer object
on heap"] W -->|"unboxing
intValue()"| P2["int 5
primitive on stack"] ``` Autoboxing wraps a primitive into a heap object. Unboxing extracts the value back. Both happen silently — the compiler inserts these calls wherever the type system requires them.

sections.title: Where Autoboxing Happens — and Where It Bites You
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Assuming autoboxing is free** — every box is a `new` heap object (outside the `-128` to `127` cache); a loop that boxes a million times creates a million objects and real GC churn.
- **Unboxing a `null` without thinking** — `int y = someInteger` compiles fine but throws `NullPointerException` at runtime if the wrapper is `null`; the crash hides inside the inserted `intValue()` call.
- **Mixing `int` and `Integer` in hot paths** — using `ArrayList<Integer>` for heavy number-crunching boxes on every `add()` and unboxes on every `get()`; switch to `int[]` or `IntStream` when throughput matters.
- **Comparing wrappers with `==`** — `==` checks object identity, not value, so it works only by luck inside the cache range; use `.equals()` for `Integer` comparisons.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Autoboxing = `Integer.valueOf(int)`** — the compiler inserts this call wherever a primitive meets an object slot, like `list.add(42)`.
- **Unboxing = `intValue()`** — inserted wherever an `Integer` is used as an `int`; arithmetic, assignments, and comparisons all trigger it.
- **Collections force boxing** — you can't write `ArrayList<int>`, only `ArrayList<Integer>`, so every numeric `add()` allocates a wrapper object.
- **Unboxing `null` throws `NullPointerException`** — `int y = someInteger` becomes `someInteger.intValue()`, and `null` has no methods; this is the #1 autoboxing bug.
- **`valueOf()` caches `-128` to `127`** — boxed values in that range share one object, so `==` can pass for small numbers and fail for large ones.
- **Boxing isn't free** — each box is a heap object; in tight loops prefer `int[]` or `IntStream` over `ArrayList<Integer>` to avoid GC pressure.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
The thing to get across is that **none of this is free**, even though it looks invisible. Every time you write `Integer x = 5`, the compiler quietly rewrites it to `Integer.valueOf(5)`, and every time you use that wrapper as a number — say `int y = x` — it inserts `x.intValue()`. So boxing and unboxing are **real method calls and real heap allocations** hiding behind ordinary-looking syntax.

Where it actually shows up is collections. You can't write `ArrayList<int>`, only `ArrayList<Integer>`, so every `list.add(42)` boxes a primitive into a new object. In a tight loop doing millions of operations, that's **millions of throwaway objects and real GC pressure** — which is why I'd reach for an `int[]` or an `IntStream` when performance matters.

The detail I'd be sure to mention is the failure mode: unboxing a `null` `Integer` throws a `NullPointerException`. A line like `int total = someInteger` becomes `someInteger.intValue()`, and if that wrapper is `null` you crash — on what reads like a plain assignment with no method call in sight.

So my take: autoboxing is a great convenience for readability, but I treat any `int`-to-`Integer` boundary as two things to watch — an allocation and a possible `null`.

questions.question: How can autoboxing cause a NullPointerException in Java?
questions.title: Autoboxing NullPointerException
questions.direct_answer: When Java unboxes a `null` wrapper object to a primitive, it calls `.intValue()` (or similar) on `null` — which throws a `NullPointerException`. This happens silently in arithmetic expressions, method calls, return statements, and `switch` statements involving `Integer`, `Long`, or other wrapper types.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can identify the subtle unboxing NPE — it doesn't look like a null access from the code, which is what makes it tricky.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking NPE from autoboxing requires explicit method calls on null. It happens implicitly wherever a wrapper is used where a primitive is expected.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a real-world example: a method returning Integer can return null, and if you assign it directly to int the caller crashes. Or a HashMap.get() returns Integer — if the key is absent you get null, and using it in arithmetic blows up.

sections.title: The NPE That Looks Like It Has Nothing to Do with Null
sections.content:
Autoboxing causes a `NullPointerException` when Java tries to **unbox a `null` wrapper into a primitive** — it inserts a hidden `.intValue()` call, and calling a method on `null` crashes.

Why this exists at all: unboxing is the compiler's job, not yours. When a wrapper like `Integer` is used where an `int` is expected, the compiler quietly adds the `.intValue()` call needed to extract the number. That convenience is also the trap — because `null` is a perfectly valid value for an `Integer`, and `null.intValue()` has nowhere to go.

How it slips past you: there's no obvious null access in the code. You see a line like `int total = getScore();` where `getScore()` returns `Integer`. No `.` operator, no method call — just an assignment. Under the hood the compiler rewrote it to `int total = getScore().intValue()`, so when `getScore()` returns `null`, that's the `NullPointerException`.

The nuance is that this same hidden unboxing happens in more places than you'd expect:
- **Method returns `Integer`, caller assigns to `int`**: `int x = methodThatReturnsInteger()` — `null` return means NPE.
- **`HashMap.get()` used directly as `int`**: `int count = map.get(key)` — an absent key returns `null`, then NPE.
- **Arithmetic with a wrapper**: `Integer a = null; int sum = a + 5;` — NPE on the `+` operator, because `+` needs the primitive first.
- **`switch` on an `Integer`**: `Integer x = null; switch (x)` — `x` is unboxed before any `case` is checked, so it throws before your logic runs.

The gotcha to remember: any wrapper used where a primitive is expected is a possible `NullPointerException`, even when the line contains no visible `.` at all.

sections.title: How a null Integer Turns Into an NPE
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart LR A["Integer n = null"] --> B["int y = n"] B -->|"compiler inserts
n.intValue()"| C["call intValue()
on a null reference"] C --> D["NullPointerException"] ``` The assignment looks harmless, but the compiler-inserted `intValue()` call runs against `null` — and that is where it throws.

sections.title: Four Ways the Null Unboxing NPE Appears
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking the NPE needs a visible method call** — there's no `.` on `int x = getValue()`, yet the hidden `intValue()` is exactly where it throws.
- **Using `map.get(key)` straight as an `int`** — a missing key returns `null`, which unboxes to a `NullPointerException`; reach for `getOrDefault(key, 0)` instead.
- **Forgetting `switch` unboxes first** — `switch (nullInteger)` throws before any `case` runs, so null-check the wrapper before switching on it.
- **Returning a `null` `Integer` from an API** — it pushes the unboxing trap onto every caller; prefer a sentinel value, a primitive return, or `OptionalInt`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Root cause: `intValue()` on `null`** — unboxing a `null` wrapper calls a method on nothing, throwing `NullPointerException`.
- **The line looks innocent** — `int x = getCount()` has no visible `.` or `null`, yet the compiler hides a `.intValue()` call that crashes.
- **`map.get(missingKey)` returns `null`** — assigning that straight to an `int` is the most common real-world trigger; use `getOrDefault(key, 0)`.
- **Arithmetic unboxes too** — `Integer a = null; a + 5` fails on the `+`, because the operator needs the primitive value first.
- **`switch` on a `null` `Integer`** — the value is unboxed before any `case` is checked, so it throws before your code runs.
- **Fix by null-checking or defaulting** — `n != null ? n : 0`, `getOrDefault()`, or `Objects.requireNonNullElse(n, 0)` (Java 9+).

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
What makes this bug nasty is that **it doesn't look like a null bug**. There's no `.` operator on the line, no obvious method call — just something like `int total = getScore()` where `getScore()` returns an `Integer`. The compiler silently turns that into `getScore().intValue()`, so when the method hands back `null`, you get a `NullPointerException` on a line that reads like a simple assignment.

The most common place I've seen this is **maps**. `map.get(key)` returns `null` when the key is absent, and if you assign it straight to an `int`, it unboxes `null` and blows up. The fix is `map.getOrDefault(key, 0)`, which never returns `null`. It also hides in arithmetic — `Integer a = null; a + 5` fails on the `+` because the operator needs the primitive first — and in `switch`, where a `null` `Integer` is unboxed before any `case` is even checked.

> Any wrapper used where a primitive is expected is a potential `NullPointerException`.

So the way I defend against it: null-check before unboxing, lean on `getOrDefault()` for maps, or use `Objects.requireNonNullElse(n, 0)` from Java 9. And where I control the API, I avoid returning a `null` `Integer` in the first place — a sentinel or `OptionalInt` saves every caller from this trap.

questions.question: What is the Integer cache in Java and why does it cause == comparison bugs?
questions.title: The Integer Cache and == Comparison Bug
questions.direct_answer: Java caches `Integer` objects for values **-128 to 127**. When you autobox an `int` in this range, `Integer.valueOf()` returns the same cached object every time. For values outside this range, a new object is created each time. This means `Integer a = 127; Integer b = 127; a == b` is `true`, but `Integer a = 128; Integer b = 128; a == b` is `false` — even though the values are equal.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know this specific JVM behaviour and can explain why == on Integer gives inconsistent results depending on the value.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using == to compare Integer objects expecting it to work like == on int. == on objects always compares addresses, not values.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: The cache size (-128 to 127) can be extended via JVM flag -XX:AutoBoxCacheMax=N. Also: the same caching exists for Byte (all 256 values), Short (-128 to 127), Long (-128 to 127), Boolean (true/false), and Character (0 to 127).

sections.title: The JVM Reuses Small Integer Objects — But Not Large Ones
sections.content:
The **Integer cache** is a pool of pre-created `Integer` objects that Java keeps for values `-128` to `127`. Autoboxing an `int` in that range hands back a shared object; outside it, you get a brand-new object every time.

Why does this exist? Performance. Small integers show up constantly — loop counters, flags, sizes — so the JVM pre-builds the common ones once and reuses them instead of allocating a fresh object on every box. It's a sensible optimization that happens to create a famously confusing side effect.

How it actually works: `Integer.valueOf(n)` — the method autoboxing calls — checks the value first. For `-128` to `127` it returns the same cached instance, so calling `Integer.valueOf(100)` ten times gives you the same heap object ten times. For anything outside that window it runs `new Integer(...)`, so two calls to `Integer.valueOf(200)` produce two different objects.

Now the nuance that trips people up. You already know `==` on objects compares memory addresses, not values. Combine that with the cache and you get inconsistent results from identical-looking code: `Integer a = 127; Integer b = 127; a == b` is `true` because both point at the same cached object — but `Integer a = 128; Integer b = 128; a == b` is `false` because each is a separate object. The code is the same; only the value changed.

The gotcha and the fix are one rule: **never compare `Integer` with `==`, always use `.equals()`**. `.equals()` compares the numeric value regardless of object identity, so the cache boundary stops mattering. The same caching exists for `Byte` (all values), `Short` (`-128` to `127`), `Long` (`-128` to `127`), `Boolean`, and `Character` (`0` to `127`).

sections.title: valueOf() With and Without the Cache
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TD A["Integer.valueOf(n)"] --> B{"is n between
-128 and 127?"} B -->|"yes"| C["return cached object
same instance every call"] B -->|"no"| D["create new Integer object
new instance each call"] C --> E["a == b is TRUE
same cached object"] D --> F["a == b is FALSE
different heap objects"] ``` The branch on the value is the whole story: inside the window you reuse one object, outside it you allocate a new one each time — and `==` reports identity, not equality.

sections.title: The == Inconsistency at the Cache Boundary
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using `==` to compare `Integer` values** — it compares references, so it passes for `127` and fails for `128`; the bug is invisible until your data crosses the cache boundary.
- **Assuming the cache covers all small numbers** — it stops at `127`; `128` and above always allocate fresh objects, so `==` flips to `false` there.
- **Trusting `==` because the tests passed** — tests with small values fall inside `-128` to `127` and pass by accident, hiding the bug until production data goes higher.
- **Raising `-XX:AutoBoxCacheMax` to make `==` work** — it only moves the boundary, it doesn't fix identity-vs-value comparison; use `.equals()` instead.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Cache range is `-128` to `127`** — `Integer.valueOf()` returns the same pooled object for every value in this range.
- **Outside the range = new object each call** — `Integer.valueOf(128)` allocates fresh, so two equal values are different references.
- **`==` compares references, not values** — that's why `127 == 127` is `true` but `128 == 128` is `false` for boxed `Integer`.
- **Always use `.equals()` for `Integer`** — it compares numeric value regardless of identity; `==` only ever works by accident.
- **Same caching in other wrappers** — `Byte` (all values), `Short` and `Long` (`-128` to `127`), `Boolean`, and `Character` (`0` to `127`).
- **Upper bound is tunable** — `-XX:AutoBoxCacheMax=N` raises the `Integer` cache ceiling, but the rule never changes: compare with `.equals()`.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
The key insight is that two `Integer` variables holding the same number can be `==` or not, depending on the value — and that's not random, it's the cache. Java's `Integer.valueOf()`, the method autoboxing calls, keeps a pool of objects for `-128` to `127`. Box `100` twice and you get the same object back, so `==` is `true`. Box `200` twice and you get two separate objects, so `==` is `false` even though the values match.

That's the trap: people use `==` on `Integer` expecting it to compare values the way it does on `int`. On objects, `==` always compares references, so it only works by accident inside the cache window and silently breaks the moment a value crosses `127`. The rule I'd state plainly is: **always compare `Integer` with `.equals()`, never `==`**.

A couple of things that show depth here. The same caching exists for `Byte` — all of its values — plus `Short`, `Long`, `Boolean`, and `Character` from `0` to `127`. And the upper bound is configurable with the JVM flag `-XX:AutoBoxCacheMax=N`.

But I wouldn't lean on any of that. The robust answer is **value-based comparison**: use `.equals()` and the cache boundary stops mattering at all.
